Archaeology Finds

Real archaeological finds — from ancient Israel through the early Christian centuries. Each card separates what the find shows, what scholars infer, and what is still debated. Photos stay in the repo with credit and license under each image.

Ancient Israel Gospels world AD 30–70 AD 70–150 AD 150–325 AD 325–1000

Ancient Israel & the Second Temple

Finds from early Israel through the Second Temple — Bible book and chapter references only, never verse text. Subgroups run Early Israel → Kingdoms → Exile & return → Second Temple.

Bronze Age / early Israel

Merneptah Stele (Israel Stele)

inscription / victory stele

c. 1208–1207 BCE (Merneptah year 5); discovered 1896

A tall black granite victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah. Near the end it lists Canaanite places and a people written with the determinative for a people-group, widely read as Israel — the earliest widely accepted extrabiblical reference.

Found: Thebes (Egypt), in Merneptah’s mortuary temple; Flinders Petrie · Now: Egyptian Museum, Cairo

Bible: Exodus 1; Joshua 1; Judges 1

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: An Egyptian royal inscription of Merneptah’s fifth year names a people in Canaan that the majority of Egyptologists read as Israel, marked as a people rather than a city.

Scholars infer: Israel was already an identifiable sedentary/agricultural people in Canaan by the late 13th century BCE.

Still debated: Exact social shape of that early Israel; a separate Berlin pedestal fragment proposed as an earlier ‘Israel’ remains contested.

Source ↗ Commons ↗ Commons ↗

Gezer calendar

inscription / limestone tablet

Usually late 10th / early 9th century BCE (Iron Age IIA)

A small limestone tablet listing a yearly round of agricultural tasks in early Hebrew script — months for sowing, harvesting, and fruit. A concrete window onto farm life, not kings or battles.

Found: Tel Gezer, Israel (Macalister excavations, 1908) · Now: Istanbul Archaeology Museums (Museum of the Ancient Orient)

Bible: 1 Kings 9:15-17; Joshua 10:33; Judges 1:29

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: An Iron Age school-exercise or farm calendar from Gezer uses an early Canaanite/Hebrew alphabet to list seasonal farm work.

Scholars infer: Literacy and scribal practice in the highland/lowland border zone earlier than many once assumed.

Still debated: Exact language classification (Hebrew vs. related Canaanite dialect); precise century within Iron IIA.

Commons ↗

Khirbet Qeiyafa ostracon

ostracon / ink inscription

c. late 11th–early 10th century BCE (excavators); readings debated

ⓘ Read with care

Text readings and the site’s link to biblical Shaaraim are still debated among epigraphers.

A five-line ink text on a pottery sherd from a strong early Iron Age fortress. Scholars disagree on the exact reading, but many see an early Hebrew social or ethical text from the time of emerging Judah.

Found: Khirbet Qeiyafa, Israel (excavated by Garfinkel & Ganor) · Now: Israel Antiquities Authority / displayed at Bible Lands Museum / Israel Museum contexts

Bible: 1 Samuel 17:1-3; Joshua 15:36

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A substantial ink inscription existed at Qeiyafa in the early Iron Age; the site was a planned fortified town.

Scholars infer: Some level of administration and literacy in Judah’s formative period; possible links to biblical Elah Valley geography.

Still debated: Full decipherment of the lines; whether the site is biblical Shaaraim; how ‘Hebrew’ the language is.

Commons ↗

Kingdoms of Israel and Judah

Tel Dan Stele (‘House of David’)

inscription / basalt victory stele

9th century BCE (often linked to Hazael of Aram; fragments found 1993–94)

Broken basalt pieces of an Aramaic victory inscription. One phrase is widely read as bytdwd — ‘House of David’ — the earliest clear extrabiblical mention of David’s dynasty.

Found: Tel Dan, northern Israel (secondary use in a wall) · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (IAA collection)

Bible: 2 Samuel 5:1-5; 2 Kings 8:28-29; 2 Kings 9:14-16

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A 9th-century Aramaic royal inscription from Dan refers to a Judahite royal house written as bytdwd.

Scholars infer: David was remembered as a dynastic founder by neighboring kingdoms within about a century or two of the biblical United Monarchy traditions.

Still debated: Whether the author is certainly Hazael; exact restoration of damaged lines; minority alternative readings of bytdwd.

Source ↗ Israel Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone)

inscription / basalt stele

9th century BCE (Louvre: era of Mesha c. 830–805 BCE); found 1868

ⓘ Read with care

The stele is solid; whether line 31 names the “House of David” is still debated after new imaging.

King Mesha of Moab tells, in Moabite closely related to Hebrew, how he threw off Israel’s yoke after Omri’s oppression, took towns, and dragged vessels of YHWH before Chemosh. A rare enemy-king’s version of the same world as 2 Kings.

Found: Dhiban (biblical Dibon), Jordan · Now: Musée du Louvre, Paris (AO 5066)

Bible: 2 Kings 3:4-27; 1 Kings 16:21-28; Numbers 21:26-30

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Mesha names Omri, Israel, YHWH, and Moabite reconquest of territory east of the Dead Sea in the 9th century.

Scholars infer: How the Moabite and biblical accounts relate (parallel conflicts vs. the same war); possible ‘House of David’ reading in a damaged line.

Still debated: Reading of line 31 (House of David vs. alternatives); exact sync with 2 Kings 3.

Louvre ↗ Commons ↗

Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (Jehu panel)

inscription / carved obelisk

Erected c. 825 BCE; Jehu tribute scene ~841 BCE

A black limestone Assyrian obelisk. One register labels Jehu of the ‘House of Omri’ bowing before Shalmaneser III — the only surviving ancient image of an Israelite king, caught mid-prostration with tribute.

Found: Nimrud (Kalhu), Iraq · Now: British Museum, London

Bible: 2 Kings 9:1-13; 2 Kings 10:31-36

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Assyria recorded Jehu (or his envoy) paying tribute and called his realm Bit-Humri (House of Omri).

Scholars infer: Jehu sought Assyrian backing amid Aramean pressure; the Bible’s silence on this tribute is political, not ignorance of Assyria.

Still debated: Whether the bowing figure is Jehu himself or a representative; how to sync with biblical chronology of Jehu’s coup.

British Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions

inscription / pithos drawings & blessings

Late 9th–early 8th century BCE (radiocarbon often ~820–745 BCE)

ⓘ Read with care

The site is real; what “YHWH and his asherah” meant in popular religion is still heavily debated.

Ink blessings and drawings on large storage jars from a desert waystation. One blessing invokes ‘YHWH of Samaria and his asherah’ — a startling glimpse of popular religion beside official Judahite monotheizing traditions.

Found: Kuntillet Ajrud (Horvat Teman), northeastern Sinai · Now: Israel Antiquities Authority collections (site finds)

Bible: 1 Kings 16:29-33; 2 Kings 17:7-12; Deuteronomy 16:21

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: 8th-century travelers/officials wrote blessings naming YHWH (of Samaria/Teman) together with ‘his asherah’.

Scholars infer: Diverse Yahwistic practice in the northern kingdom’s orbit; possible military/trade outpost with cultic space.

Still debated: Whether ‘asherah’ means the goddess or a cult symbol/pole; whether nearby Bes-like figures belong to the blessing; site function.

Commons ↗

Lachish reliefs (Sennacherib’s palace)

palace relief / siege narrative

Carved c. 700–692 BCE; depicts 701 BCE siege

Gypsum wall panels showing Assyrian troops storming Lachish: siege ramps, deportees, and the city’s fall. Jerusalem is not shown — Sennacherib preferred to advertise the city he actually took.

Found: South-West Palace of Sennacherib, Nineveh (Room 36) · Now: British Museum, London

Bible: 2 Kings 18:13-17; 2 Chronicles 32:9; Isaiah 36:1-2; Jeremiah 34:7

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Assyria celebrated the capture of Lachish in monumental art matching archaeology at Tell ed-Duweir.

Scholars infer: Lachish was Judah’s key fortress after Jerusalem; the reliefs propagandize a hard-won victory.

Still debated: Fine points of siege sequence vs. excavation layers; how many deportees the numbers imply.

British Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Sennacherib Prism (Taylor Prism)

clay prism / royal annals

c. 691 BCE (records 701 BCE campaign)

A six-sided clay prism of Sennacherib’s campaigns. Of Judah he boasts that he took 46 fortified cities and shut Hezekiah in Jerusalem ‘like a bird in a cage’ — without claiming he captured the capital.

Found: Nineveh area (Nebi Yunus); acquired via Col. Taylor · Now: British Museum, London

Bible: 2 Kings 18:13-19:37; Isaiah 36-37; 2 Chronicles 32:1-23

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Assyrian annals name Hezekiah of Judah, list massive tribute, and stop short of saying Jerusalem fell.

Scholars infer: Jerusalem survived 701 BCE under siege/pressure; biblical and Assyrian accounts share a core event while spinning outcomes differently.

Still debated: Whether a plague, tribute, or Egyptian diversion ended the campaign; sync of biblical ‘angel’ tradition with Assyrian silence.

British Museum ↗ Israel Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Siloam inscription

inscription / rock-cut Hebrew text

Late 8th century BCE (commonly linked to Hezekiah; removed 1890)

A Hebrew inscription celebrating how two crews digging from opposite ends of a water tunnel heard each other and broke through. Human, technical, almost diary-like — not a royal boast.

Found: Hezekiah’s Tunnel / Siloam Tunnel, Jerusalem · Now: Museum of the Ancient Orient, Istanbul

Bible: 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:2-4; 2 Chronicles 32:30; Isaiah 22:9-11

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Judahite workers cut a long water tunnel under Jerusalem and commemorated the breakthrough in classical biblical-period Hebrew.

Scholars infer: Usually tied to Hezekiah’s water preparations before Assyria’s 701 campaign (2 Kings 20:20).

Still debated: Some propose a slightly earlier or later cutting; exact engineering method of the snaking path.

Commons ↗

Hezekiah’s Tunnel (Siloam Tunnel)

site / engineered water tunnel

Late 8th century BCE (commonly Hezekiah); still walkable

A ~533-meter rock-cut tunnel that still carries water from the Gihon spring to Siloam. Visitors can wade it today — the same channel the Siloam inscription describes.

Found: Jerusalem — from Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam · Now: In situ (archaeological park / City of David)

Bible: 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: An Iron Age water system re-routed Jerusalem’s spring inside the walls via a hand-cut tunnel.

Scholars infer: Built to secure water under Assyrian threat in Hezekiah’s reign.

Still debated: Precise dating within the late Iron Age; relationship of Channel II and other waterworks.

Commons ↗

Ketef Hinnom silver amulets (priestly blessing)

amulet / silver scrolls

Late 7th / early 6th century BCE (Israel Museum: 6th century BCE)

Two tiny silver scrolls worn as amulets, inscribed with a blessing that matches Numbers 6:24–26. Unrolled with immense care; letters thinner than a hair. Personal piety you could wear around your neck.

Found: Ketef Hinnom burial caves, Jerusalem (Gabriel Barkay, 1979) · Now: Israel Museum / IAA (IAA 1980-1495, 1980-1496)

Bible: Numbers 6:22-27

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Pre-exilic Jerusalemites used a YHWH blessing text closely matching the priestly benediction later preserved in Numbers.

Scholars infer: The blessing circulated as liturgy/amulet before (or as) its embedding in the biblical book.

Still debated: Exact year within late Iron II; how much of each amulet is quotation vs. freer blessing formula.

Israel Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Hezekiah royal seal impression (bulla)

seal impression / clay bulla

Late 8th century BCE (reign of Hezekiah)

ⓘ Read with care

Prefer the excavated Ophel bulla; lookalikes without a dig findspot need extra care.

A clay seal impression reading roughly ‘Belonging to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah,’ with a winged sun disk. Tiny bureaucracy: the king’s office stamped papyrus documents.

Found: Ophel, Jerusalem (Eilat Mazar excavations; others known from market) · Now: IAA / displayed in Israel Museum contexts

Bible: 2 Kings 18:1-3; Isaiah 36:1; 2 Chronicles 29:1

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Official seals of Hezekiah son of Ahaz were used on documents in late-8th-century Jerusalem.

Scholars infer: A royal administration matching biblical royal names and titles.

Still debated: Iconography (Egyptianizing winged sun); status of earlier unprovenanced Hezekiah bullae vs. the excavated Ophel example.

Commons ↗

Gemariah son of Shaphan bulla

seal impression / clay bulla

Late 7th–early 6th century BCE (pre-586 destruction layer)

A stratified bulla naming Gemariah son of Shaphan — a scribe’s family known from Jeremiah’s circle. Unlike many Bible-name seals, this one came out of the dirt of Jerusalem, not a dealer’s tray.

Found: City of David, Jerusalem (Shiloh excavations) · Now: IAA / Israel Museum display contexts

Bible: Jeremiah 36:10-12; Jeremiah 36:25

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Jerusalem official named Gemariah son of Shaphan sealed documents before the Babylonian destruction.

Scholars infer: Likely the same bureaucratic family circle reflected in Jeremiah 36.

Still debated: Whether every biblical namesake is the same individual (common names); still far stronger than unprovenanced parallels.

Source ↗

Baruch (Berekhyahu) son of Neriah bullae

seal impression / clay bulla (unprovenanced)

Claimed late 7th–early 6th century BCE; authenticity disputed

ⓘ Read with care

Unprovenanced; the forgery debate is unresolved — include tagged, not as proof.

Bullae reading ‘Belonging to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe’ — the name of Jeremiah’s secretary. Electrifying if genuine; tainted because they never came from a dig.

Found: Antiquities market (unprovenanced) · Now: Private collections / published exemplars

Bible: Jeremiah 36:4-8; Jeremiah 45:1-2

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Published objects exist with that reading; they lack archaeological findspot.

Scholars infer: If genuine, they would name Baruch the scribe; that ‘if’ is the whole problem.

Still debated: Authenticity: some lab work claimed modern forgery; rejoinders say forgery is unproven. Acquittal in related trials did not prove authenticity.

Source ↗

Exile and return

Babylonian Chronicle (Jerusalem 597 BCE)

clay tablet / chronicle

Records 605–594 BCE (tablet BM 21946); Nebuchadnezzar’s 597 capture of Jerusalem

A Babylonian chronicle tablet notes that in Nebuchadnezzar’s seventh year he marched to Hatti, besieged ‘the city of Judah,’ captured the king, appointed another, and took heavy tribute — the 597 BCE deportation that took Jehoiachin.

Found: Babylon region; acquired by British Museum · Now: British Museum, London (BM 21946)

Bible: 2 Kings 24:10-17; 2 Chronicles 36:9-10; Jeremiah 22:24-30

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Babylon dated and recorded the 597 capture of Jerusalem and replacement of its king independently of the Bible.

Scholars infer: Sync point for biblical and Babylonian chronologies of the exile’s first wave.

Still debated: Fine calendar conversions; the tablet does not name Jehoiachin explicitly (other texts do).

British Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Jehoiachin ration tablets

clay tablet / palace ration list

c. 592–569 BCE (Nebuchadnezzar’s palace archives)

Cuneiform ration lists issue oil to ‘Ya’u-kīnu, king of the land of Yahudu’ and his sons — Jehoiachin living as a captive royal in Babylon, still titled king, still eating.

Found: Babylon (palace/administrative archives) · Now: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin

Bible: 2 Kings 24:12-15; 2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Babylonian accountants issued oil rations to Jehoiachin of Judah and his household in exile.

Scholars infer: Judah’s captive king retained recognized status; matches 2 Kings 25:27–30’s later elevation under Evil-merodach.

Still debated: Exact years of each tablet; how large the Judean community around him was.

Source ↗ Commons ↗

Ishtar Gate (Babylon)

monumental gate / glazed brick

Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 605–562 BCE); reconstructed display 20th century

ⓘ Read with care

Babylonian imperial architecture that sets the exile scene — not an Israelite artifact.

The dazzling blue-glazed processional gate of Nebuchadnezzar’s Babylon, with striding lions, dragons, and bulls. Not a ‘Bible object’ — it is the empire’s front door, the built world of the exile.

Found: Babylon, Iraq (Koldewey excavations) · Now: Pergamonmuseum / Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin

Bible: 2 Kings 24:10-16; Psalm 137:1; Daniel 1:1-4

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Nebuchadnezzar built a monumental Ishtar Gate and processional way in glazed brick.

Scholars infer: Visual scale of the capital that held Judean deportees and palace captives like Jehoiachin.

Still debated: None about authenticity; modern reconstruction height/arrangement details vary by gallery.

Commons ↗

Cyrus Cylinder

clay cylinder / foundation inscription

After 539 BCE (Cyrus’s capture of Babylon)

Cyrus presents himself (in Babylonian voice) as Marduk’s chosen restorer: temples repaired, deported gods and people sent home. It never names Judah — but it shows the imperial policy climate behind Ezra’s return story.

Found: Babylon (Amran / Esagila area), 1879 (Hormuzd Rassam) · Now: British Museum, London

Bible: Ezra 1:1-4; 2 Chronicles 36:22-23; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Cyrus claimed a policy of restoring cults and returning deportees after taking Babylon in 539 BCE.

Scholars infer: Judean return and temple rebuilding fit a wider Achaemenid pattern; biblical ‘decree’ language is a Judean theological framing of that climate.

Still debated: How closely the Cylinder maps to Ezra 1 (parallel vs. same document); ‘human rights charter’ modern slogan is anachronistic.

British Museum ↗ The Met ↗ Commons ↗

Elephantine papyri (Jewish temple in Egypt)

papyrus archive / legal & letters

5th century BCE (Persian period); temple destroyed 410 BCE

Aramaic contracts and letters from a Jewish military colony that had its own temple of YHW beside Egyptian Khnum. After locals destroyed that temple, the community wrote to Jerusalem and Samaria asking permission to rebuild — diaspora Judaism negotiating with the homeland.

Found: Elephantine Island, Aswan, Egypt · Now: Brooklyn Museum; Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung, Berlin; others

Bible: Ezra 4:1-24; Nehemiah 1:1-3; Isaiah 19:19

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Persian-period Jewish community in Egypt ran a YHW temple, kept contracts in Aramaic, and petitioned Judean/Samarian officials after 410 BCE.

Scholars infer: Second Temple–era Judaism was geographically wider and ritually more diverse than Jerusalem-only models.

Still debated: How ‘orthodox’ Elephantine practice was; relationship to biblical bans on other temples.

Brooklyn Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Second Temple

Nash Papyrus

manuscript / papyrus

Usually 2nd century BCE (pre-Dead Sea Scrolls fame)

A Hebrew papyrus with the Ten Commandments and the Shema. Before Qumran, this was the oldest known biblical manuscript — a reminder that scripture lived on fragile sheets long before bound Bibles.

Found: Egypt (purchased 1902; exact findspot uncertain) · Now: Cambridge University Library

Bible: Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21; Deuteronomy 6:4-5

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Second Temple–period Hebrew sheet combined Decalogue and Shema texts for liturgical or teaching use.

Scholars infer: Fluid textual traditions and catechetical anthologies before the later Masoretic standardization.

Still debated: Exact date within Hellenistic/early Roman centuries; whether it is a liturgical leaf or school text.

Source ↗ Commons ↗

Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ)

manuscript / parchment scroll

c. 125–100 BCE (palaeography; Israel Museum)

A complete (nearly) Book of Isaiah on parchment from the Dead Sea Scrolls — about a thousand years older than the medieval Hebrew Bibles previously used for comparison. You can see the columns, repairs, and scribe’s hand.

Found: Qumran Cave 1, Dead Sea (1947) · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book)

Bible: Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 53:1-12; Luke 4:17-19

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Second Temple Jewish community preserved Isaiah in a form remarkably close to the later medieval text, with meaningful variants.

Scholars infer: Stability and diversity both mark the Hebrew textual tradition; Qumran’s library was not a fringe oddity alone.

Still debated: Community identity (Essene vs. broader); how to weigh variants for modern Bible editions.

Israel Museum ↗ Israel Museum ↗ Commons ↗

Herodian Temple Mount masonry

architecture / ashlars

Late 1st century BCE – early 1st century CE (Herod’s expansion)

ⓘ Read with care

Jewish Second Temple masonry — context for the Temple Jesus knew, not a Christian artifact.

Enormous finely cut limestone ashlars with characteristic Herodian margins — the retaining walls of the expanded Temple platform. Touchable scale for the Second Temple Jesus knew.

Found: Jerusalem — Temple Mount retaining walls · Now: In situ (Western Wall and southern/western excavations)

Bible: Mark 13:1-2; John 2:20; Acts 3:1-2

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Herod’s engineers built monumental ashlar retaining walls still visible around the Temple Mount.

Scholars infer: Match Josephus’s descriptions of Herodian building ambition.

Still debated: Exact phasing of some courses; later rebuilds atop Herodian stone.

Commons ↗

‘Place of Trumpeting’ inscription

inscription / Hebrew stone

1st century CE (Herodian Temple period); found 1968/69

A Hebrew stone reading roughly ‘to the place of trumpeting…’ — marking where priests signaled Sabbath and festival times from the Temple’s pinnacle. The stone fell onto the street below in the Roman destruction.

Found: Southwest corner of Temple Mount / Herodian street, Jerusalem · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (replica at site)

Bible: Numbers 10:1-10; Nehemiah 12:35-36; Josephus related

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: The Herodian Temple had a designated trumpeting spot labeled in Hebrew on architecture.

Scholars infer: Matches literary notices of priestly trumpet signals for sacred time.

Still debated: Exact restoration of the broken last word; precise corner placement.

Source ↗ Commons ↗

Magdala stone

carved synagogue stone

Early 1st century CE (pre-70); found 2009

ⓘ Read with care

The Magdala synagogue context is solid; readings of the stone’s symbols still vary.

A decorated limestone block from a Galilean synagogue destroyed around the First Revolt. Reliefs may show the Temple’s menorah and sacred furniture — a village synagogue keeping Jerusalem’s Temple before its eyes.

Found: Magdala synagogue, Israel · Now: On site / Magdala archaeological park (IAA)

Bible: Matthew 15:39; Mark 8:10; Luke 8:2

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A 1st-century Galilee synagogue contained a carved stone with cultic imagery including a seven-branched menorah-like form.

Scholars infer: Strong Temple orientation in diaspora-of-the-land synagogue art before 70 CE.

Still debated: Whether the carvings depict God’s chariot, Temple utensils, or a symbolic mix; liturgical function of the stone.

Commons ↗

Arch of Titus — menorah panel

triumphal relief

Dedicated AD 81 (after Titus’s death); depicts spoils of AD 70

ⓘ Read with care

Roman propaganda after AD 70; it shows Temple vessels, not a Christian monument.

A marble relief of Roman soldiers carrying the Jerusalem Temple’s seven-branched menorah and trumpets in Titus’s triumph. The Temple’s holy things, marched through Rome — grief and proof in one panel.

Found: Via Sacra, Rome (in situ arch) · Now: In situ, Roman Forum, Rome

Bible: Exodus 25:31-40; Josephus War 7; Luke 21:5-6

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Romans depicted Temple cult objects, including a menorah, as booty from Jerusalem’s 70 CE fall.

Scholars infer: The carved menorah shape informs later Jewish art; the arch is state propaganda, not a blueprint of every Temple detail.

Still debated: How accurate the base decorations are; exact fate of the real menorah afterward.

Commons ↗

The world of the Gospels

Jewish and Roman finds that set the scene for the Gospels. These are not Christian artifacts.

Caiaphas family ossuary

everyday object / burial (Jewish context)

1st century AD (ossuary use); tomb found 1990

A limestone bone box inscribed with a name matching the high-priestly family in the Gospels. It belongs to Jewish burial practice of the Second Temple period.

Found: Peace Forest, Jerusalem · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Jerusalem ossuary of the period bears the name Joseph son of Caiaphas.

Scholars infer: Likely the high priest Joseph Caiaphas known from Josephus and the New Testament.

Still debated: Whether this exact box held the high priest himself (vs. a relative of the same name).

Commons ↗

Read the writings from this time

Pilate Stone (Caesarea inscription)

inscription (Jewish/Roman context)

AD 26–36 (Pilate’s prefecture); stone found 1961

A Latin building dedication naming “[Pon]tius Pilatus, Prefect of Judea.” It is independent Roman evidence for the prefect named in the Gospels.

Found: Caesarea Maritima, Israel · Now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (copy often displayed at Caesarea)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Roman official named Pontius Pilatus held the title prefect of Judea and dedicated a Tiberieum at Caesarea.

Scholars infer: Usual reconstruction of the damaged lines; that this is the same Pilate as in the passion narratives.

Still debated: Exact wording of some restored letters; the stone is not a Christian artifact.

Commons ↗ Britannica ↗

Read the writings from this time

Pool of Siloam

site (Jewish / Gospel-world context)

Second Temple period pool; stepped pool excavated 2004 onward

A large stepped pool fed by the Gihon spring via Hezekiah’s Tunnel. John’s Gospel places a healing of a blind man here.

Found: City of David / Silwan, Jerusalem · Now: In situ (archaeological park area)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A monumental Second Temple–period pool exists at the traditional Siloam location.

Scholars infer: This is the pool known to first-century Jerusalem and to the Johannine narrative setting.

Still debated: Full extent and phases of the complex; how visitors should picture the Gospel scene.

AD 30–70

Things people made or used in the earliest Christian years.

Capernaum “House of Peter”

house church / memorial site

1st-century house remains; Christian meeting use by ~late 1st–4th c.; octagonal memorial church later

ⓘ Read with care

Tradition links this house to Peter; archaeology shows a house later treated as sacred, but the identification with Peter himself is debated.

Excavators found a first-century house whose main room was later plastered, inscribed, and set apart, then covered by an octagonal church. Pilgrims remembered it as Peter’s home.

Found: Capernaum (Kfar Nahum), Sea of Galilee, Israel · Now: Under the modern memorial church; Franciscan Custody / IAA oversight of excavations

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Capernaum house was adapted for Christian gathering and later monumentalized.

Scholars infer: Early local memory linked the house to Peter and to Jesus’ Capernaum ministry.

Still debated: Whether the house actually belonged to Peter; how early the Christian use began.

AD 70–150

Things people made or used as the apostolic generation passed.

Rotas–Sator square (Pompeii)

graffito / word square

Before AD 79 (Pompeii burial under Vesuvius)

ⓘ Read with care

The square is real and early; whether it is Christian at all is still debated.

A five-word Latin palindrome square (ROTAS OPERA TENET AREPO SATOR). Some read a hidden Christian prayer; others see a pagan word-play or magic square.

Found: Pompeii (Palaestra / related finds) · Now: In situ / Pompeii archaeological site documentation; casts and photos widely published

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: The square existed in the Vesuvian cities before 79.

Scholars infer: Possible early Christian presence — or none.

Still debated: Whether the Pompeii squares are Christian at all.

Commons ↗

Read the writings from this time

Rylands Papyrus P52 (John)

manuscript / papyrus

Often placed early–mid 2nd century; some scholars prefer later 2nd / ~200

A tiny scrap of a papyrus codex with John 18 on both sides. It is among the earliest surviving pieces of any New Testament book.

Found: Egypt (acquired early 20th c.; exact find-spot uncertain) · Now: John Rylands Library, University of Manchester

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A Greek copy of John’s Gospel circulated in Egypt in a codex format by roughly the 2nd century.

Scholars infer: How early John was composed and how fast it spread; that Christians preferred the codex early.

Still debated: Exact date within the 2nd century (or slightly later).

AD 150–325

Things people made or used before Constantine.

Alexamenos graffito

graffito

Usually late 1st–early 3rd century (often ~AD 200)

A scratched cartoon of a person raising a hand toward a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, with Greek words mocking “Alexamenos” for worshipping his god. One of the earliest pictures of a crucifixion scene.

Found: Palatine Hill, Rome (paedagogium) · Now: Palatine Museum, Rome

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: Someone in Rome mocked a person named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified god.

Scholars infer: The mocked figure is Jesus; the joke reflects pagan contempt for the cross.

Still debated: Exact date; whether the donkey-head is a specific anti-Jewish/anti-Christian slur tradition.

inscription

Late 2nd / early 3rd century (Vatican Museums)

A Greek verse epitaph in coded Christian language: a “holy Shepherd,” travel to Rome, “pure fish,” bread and wine. The Vatican calls it the most ancient known Christian inscription.

Found: Hieropolis (Hierapolis area), Phrygia, Turkey — reused in a bath building · Now: Vatican Museums, Museo Pio Cristiano

Scholars infer: Abercius was a bishop of Hierapolis; the “queen” is the Roman church.

St Peter’s tomb area (Vatican necropolis / scavi)

basilica / tomb site

2nd-century shrine (“Trophy of Gaius”); Constantinian basilica above; excavations 1939–

ⓘ Read with care

A second-century memorial on this spot is well established; whether particular bones are Peter’s remains is still debated.

Excavations under the high altar revealed a pagan necropolis and a second-century memorial traditionally linked to Peter’s grave, later enclosed by Constantine’s basilica.

Found: Under St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City · Now: Vatican scavi (guided access)

Evidence shows / Scholars infer / Still debated

Evidence shows: A carefully marked memorial stood on this spot by the 2nd century; Constantine built directly over it.

Scholars infer: Early Roman Christian memory of Peter’s burial here (cf. Gaius in Eusebius).

Still debated: Identification of specific bones as Peter’s; reading of some graffiti (“Petros eni”).
